study.title: 2 Samuel 13 Violence in the house of David and the weight of a disbanded family
study.overview: This chapter narrates a painful sequence of sin, manipulation, violence, silence and revenge within the royal family. Amnom desires Tamar in a disorderly manner, uses Jonadab's perverse council to lure her, the violent and then reject her with contempt. Tamar is humiliated and lives desolate with Absalom. David is angry, but does not apply immediate justice. Two years later, Absalom plans and executes Amnon's death, triggering alarm in Jerusalem. The chapter ends with David's grief and his longing for Absalom, despite his absence for three years in Gesur.

outline.title: Amnom's disorderly desire and Jonadabe's plan
outline.explanation: Amnom is consumed by Tamar, but not with holy love; the text shows a sick obsession. Jonadab, described as very cunning, creates a strategy to put Tamar vulnerable before Amnon, using the king's confidence and the naivety of the young man.

outline.title: The violation of Tamar
outline.explanation: David sends Tamar to serve his brother, and Amnon isolates, coage, and strength despite his resistance. Tamar appeals to honor, the order of Israel and the possibility of marriage, but he ignores it. The narrative highlights the brutality of the act and her inability to prevent evil.

outline.title: The contempt of Amnon, the pain of Tamar and the wrath of David
outline.explanation: Soon after raping her, Amnom hates her and expells her, aggravating humiliation. Tamar tears her clothes in colors, puts gray on her head and cries; Absalom notices what has happened and tries to silence her. David hears everything and angers, but the chapter does not record punishment for Amnon.

outline.title: The Revenge of Absalom and David's mourning
outline.explanation: After two years, Absalom organizes a feast of shearing, attracts Amnom and sends him to kill him. The exaggerated rumor causes panic in David, but Jonadab clarifies that only Amnon died. Absalom flees to Geshur, he stays there three years, and David weeps for Amnon and then wishes to see Absalom again.

study.context: The chapter itself is linked to the previous announcement that the Lord would raise evil from David's own house as a discipline for sin committed with Bathsheba and Uriah. The commentators' notes understand this episode as the beginning of this domestic suffering. Also appears the custom of sheep shearing as an occasion for meeting and feast, used by Absalom to execute his plan.
study.theology: The text shows how sexual sin, manipulation and lack of correction generate a chain of destruction within the family. Amnom's passion is not presented as true love, but as an illicit and destructive desire. Tamar speaks with moral clarity: she appeals to what is right in Israel, showing that violence against it was not only personal, but also an affront to the moral order of the people. The chapter also highlights the guilt aggravated by silence and omission: David angers, but we do not see immediate justice; Absalom represses pain and turns it into revenge; the result is death, mourning and distancing. There is also an aspect of divine discipline over the house of David, without this suffocating the human agents of their moral responsibility. The end of the chapter mixes sadness and paternal affection, but this affection appears disorderly and insufficient to restore justice.

scholarViews.insight: Amnom had no legitimate love for Tamar, but an erotic obsession with sickness; the note highlights that he wanted to sexually possess his sister, not marry her.

The commentary understands this episode as the beginning of the punishment announced to David, by which evils arise from his own house, showing the connection between the king's sin and disorder among his sons.
The note notes that Tamar was Absalom's blood sister, but only Amnon's half-sister, and that this kinship relationship helps explain the social and family severity of the episode.

questions: What signs does the text give that Amnon's feeling was not love, but a disorderly and possessive desire?
Why does David's reaction, though just in his indignation, seem insufficient to curb the escalation of evil within the family?
How does Tamar's pain and Absalom's revenge show that the absence of justice can multiply injustice?
study.practice: This chapter calls the community of faith to treat sin seriously, to protect the vulnerable and not to confuse passion with love. It also exhorts parents, leaders and family members not to respond to evil only with emotion, but with justice, truth and responsibility. For practical life, it is a warning against manipulation, against accomplice silence and against revenge of reparation. Instead, God's people must seek acceptance for the victim, correction for the aggressor and confidence that the Lord sees the evil that men hide.
study.uncertainty: The notes mention a textual variant in verse 39, in which some traditions differently read the expression about the king; this does not alter the general sense of the closing of the chapter. There are also, in the notes, interpretive readings about the motivations of David and Absalom that should be read as hypotheses, not as definitive statements of the text.
